text_notes: Corrected one Wikisource typo, قفسں to قفس (stanza 2, line 6). Diacritics kept as in the source.

overview.summary: A caged bird remembers the lost freedom and beauty of its garden, nest, and beloved companion. It contrasts that past with its present dark cage, where it fears dying of grief. Finally it asks listeners not to mistake its cry for a song and begs the captor to set it free.
overview.speaker: The speaker is a captive bird in a cage, addressing its own memory, God, human listeners, and finally the captor.
overview.form: The poem is a three-stanza nazm with unequal stanza lengths of 10, 6, and 6 lines; its rhyme is stanzaic rather than a single ghazal radif, using recurring end-rhymes such as -ānā in stanza 1, -ūñ/-āūñ in stanza 2, and -ai/-āle in stanza 3.

stanzas.role: This stanza establishes the remembered past of garden, nest, freedom, and the beloved, and contrasts it with the cage and the impossible wish for release.
This stanza shifts to the present misery of captivity, describing the bird's longing for home, the spring outside, and its complaint to God and fear of death.
This stanza turns the personal lament into a universal cry of wounded hearts, warns listeners not to hear it as mere song, and makes a direct appeal to the captor for freedom.

turns: Stanza 1, line 1: opening turn into nostalgic memory of the past.
Stanza 1, lines 5–6: the memory turns painful, as remembered beauty now wounds the heart.
Stanza 1, lines 9–10: shift from remembered freedom and the beloved to the present cage and the wish for release.
Stanza 2, line 1: shift to explicit present suffering and self-description as unfortunate.
Stanza 2, line 5: direct address to God with the complaint of captivity and fear of death.
Stanza 3, lines 3–4: shift from personal complaint to addressing listeners and redefining the song as a lament.
Stanza 3, lines 5–6: final direct appeal to the captor, asking for freedom as a source of blessing.
overview.readings: Beyond the literal caged bird, the poem is often read as an allegory of the human soul trapped in material existence or of a colonized people longing for political and spiritual freedom. The final plea to the captor to earn a blessing by releasing the prisoner gives the poem a moral and spiritual edge.

ur: آتا ہے یاد مجھ کو گزرا ہوا زمانا
وہ باغ کی بہاریں، وہ سب کا چہچہانا
roman: ātā hai yād mujh ko guzrā huā zamāna
vo bāġh kī bahāreñ vo sab kā chahchahānā

phrases.gloss: yād ānā: comes to memory; is remembered

poetic: I remember the bygone age—
the garden’s springtimes, the chirping of all.
notes: yād ānā is an idiom meaning to come to mind or be remembered; the remembered thing is the grammatical subject.
guzrā huā zamāna stresses an age that has passed away and cannot return.
bahāreñ, plural of bahār, means springtimes but also connotes bloom, beauty, and vitality.
sab kā chahchahānā evokes a whole garden alive with birdsong, contrasting with the cage later in the poem.
The pairing of visual bloom and audible chirping builds a full sensory memory of lost freedom.
blocks.role: Opens the poem with nostalgic remembrance of a lost garden world of spring and birdsong.

context_notes.text: bahār can mean both 'spring' and 'splendor, glory'; the English 'springtimes' loses the second sense.

ur: آزادیاں کہاں وہ اب اپنے گھونسلے کی
اپنی خوشی سے آنا، اپنی خوشی سے جانا
roman: āzādiyāñ kahāñ woh ab apne ghonsle kī
apnī khushī se ānā apnī khushī se jānā

phrases.gloss: of one's own free will; voluntarily
of one's own free will; voluntarily

poetic: Where now are those freedoms of my own nest—
to come of my own free will, to go of my own free will?
notes: The plural āzādiyāñ stresses multiple freedoms, not a single liberty.
The idiom apnī khushī se means 'of one's own free will' or 'voluntarily,' and its repetition underlines autonomy.
The nest (ghonsla) symbolizes home, safety, and belonging, later opposed to the cage (qafas).
The question with kahāñ ... ab is rhetorical: the speaker knows these freedoms are lost.
The paired infinitives ānā and jānā evoke unrestricted movement in and out of the nest.
blocks.role: It specifies the lost freedoms—coming and going from the nest at will—sharpening the contrast with the present cage.

ur: لگتی ہے چوٹ دل پر، آتا ہے یاد جس دم
شبنم کے آنسوؤں پر کلیوں کا مُسکرانا
roman: lagtī hai choṭ dil par ātā hai yād jis dam
shabnam ke ānsūoñ par kaliyoñ kā muskurānā
poetic: When memory comes, a wound strikes at the heart —
the smiling of the buds over the dew’s tears.
notes: The clause introduced by jis dam reaches into the next line: it is the remembered image of dew and buds that wounds the heart.
Dew is personified as tears and buds as smiling, a miniature remembered scene of the lost garden.
yād ānā makes remembering not neutral recollection but an event that strikes the speaker.
The contrast between remembered beauty and present pain gives the couplet its turn from nostalgia to wounding.
blocks.role: This couplet turns nostalgia into pain: the remembered smile of garden buds over dew now strikes the captive speaker's heart.

ur: وہ پیاری پیاری صورت، وہ کامنی سی مورت
آباد جس کے دم سے تھا میرا آشیانا
roman: woh pyārī pyārī sūrat woh kāminī sī mūrat
ābād jis ke dam se thā merā āshiyāna

phrases.gloss: by whose breath/presence; thanks to whom

poetic: That dear, dear face, that form like a beautiful woman—
by whose breath my nest was alive.
notes: The repeated pyārī pyārī intensifies endearment, making the remembered face doubly dear.
kāminī and mūrat are Sanskrit-derived; mūrat can mean an image or idol, giving the beloved an almost worshipped, idol-like beauty.
dam means both breath and life, so the beloved's presence was the very life of the nest.
āshiyāna is the bird's nest, the lost home now replaced by the cage.
The couplet personalizes the loss: the garden and nest were not empty but were made home by the beloved.
blocks.role: Recalls the beloved's face and form; her presence alone made the nest a living home, deepening the loss.

context_notes.text: mūrat (from Sanskrit mūrti) can mean an image, form, or idol; the word may carry an idolatrous nuance that English 'form' lacks.
dam means both 'breath' and 'life,' so 'by whose breath' also implies 'by whose life.'

ur: آتی نہیں صدائیں اُس کی مرے قفس میں
ہوتی مری رہائی اے کاش میرے بس میں!
roman: ātī nahīñ sadāeñ us kī mere qafas meñ
hotī merī rihāī ai kāsh mere bas meñ
poetic: Her calls no longer reach me in my cage
If only my release were within my power!
notes: The 'her' of 'us kī' reaches back to the beloved companion of stanza one, whose presence once made the nest alive.
'sadāeñ' can mean voices, calls, or sounds; in the cage the bird is cut off from even this trace of the beloved.
The phrase 'mere bas meñ' is an idiom meaning within one's power or control, stressing the bird's helplessness.
'ai kāsh' introduces an optative wish that the speaker knows is beyond reach.
The couplet closes the stanza by turning from remembered freedom and companionship to present captivity and the impossible longing for release.
blocks.role: Turns from memory to present cage, expressing the loss of the beloved's voice and a helpless wish for freedom.

context_notes.text: qafas (cage) is a conventional Urdu/Persian poetic motif for the soul's or a people's captivity.

ur: کیا بد نصیب ہوں مَیں گھر کو ترس رہا ہوں
ساتھی تو ہیں وطن میں، مَیں قید میں پڑا ہوں
roman: kyā bad-nasīb hūñ maiñ ghar ko taras rahā hūñ
sāthī to haiñ vatan meñ maiñ qaid meñ paṛā hūñ

phrases.gloss: am imprisoned / have fallen into captivity

poetic: How unfortunate I am—I pine for home;
my companions are in the homeland, while I lie in a cage.
notes: کیا here is exclamatory 'how', not interrogative 'what'.
بد نصیب is a compound adjective meaning ill-fated or unfortunate.
The contrast between وطن (homeland) and قید (captivity) sharpens the speaker's exile; in Iqbal, homeland can carry political resonance.
قید میں پڑا ہوں literally means 'I have fallen into captivity', using پڑنا to express a trapped state.
blocks.role: States the bird's present misery: it longs for home while companions remain free in the homeland, deepening the captivity contrast.

ur: آئی بہار، کلیاں پھُولوں کی ہنس رہی ہیں
مَیں اس اندھیرے گھر میں قسمت کو رو رہا ہوں
roman: āī bahār kaliyāñ phūloñ kī hans rahī haiñ
maiñ is andhere ghar meñ qismat ko ro rahā hūñ
poetic: Spring has arrived, and the flower-buds are laughing,
While I, in this dark house, weep over my fate.
notes: The buds' laughter personifies blooming as joy, making the caged bird's grief feel sharper.
The dark house is the cage itself, not a true home; it remains dark even as spring brightens the world outside.
The phrase 'qismat ko ro rahā hūñ' means weeping over one's fate, expressing helpless sorrow rather than anger at any person.
The couplet builds on the contrast between outer nature's renewal and the speaker's solitary darkness.
blocks.role: It sharpens the contrast between nature's renewal outside and the speaker's dark captivity, turning spring joy into personal grief.

ur: اس قید کا الٰہی! دُکھڑا کسے سُناؤں
ڈر ہے یہیں قفس میں مَیں غم سے مر نہ جاؤں
roman: is qaid kā ilāhī dukhṛā kise sunāūñ
ḍar hai yahīñ qafas meñ maiñ ġham se mar na jāūñ

phrases.gloss: to pour out one's tale of woe, tell one's sad story

poetic: O God, to whom can I tell the sorrow of this captivity?
I fear that here in this cage I may die of grief.
notes: ilāhī is a direct address to God, turning the bird's complaint into a prayer from inside captivity.
dukhṛā sunānā is an idiom meaning to pour out one's tale of woe; kise makes this an unanswerable question.
qaid and qafas both reinforce the cage motif, often read in Iqbal as political or spiritual captivity.
ḍar hai ... mar na jāūñ uses the subjunctive after fear, meaning 'I fear lest I die'.
ġham se marnā intensifies the contrast with the spring outside, as grief itself becomes a fatal force.
blocks.role: The bird voices its captivity's sorrow to God, fearing grief may kill it inside the cage, deepening present misery.

ur: جب سے چمن چھُٹا ہے، یہ حال ہو گیا ہے
دل غم کو کھا رہا ہے، غم دل کو کھا رہا ہے
roman: jab se chaman chhuṭā hai ye hāl ho gayā hai
dil ġham ko khā rahā hai ġham dil ko khā rahā hai
poetic: Ever since the garden was left behind, this has become my state—
the heart devours grief, and grief devours the heart.
notes: The couplet is built on a chiasmus: first the heart eats grief, then grief eats the heart, making the suffering self-perpetuating.
chaman chhuṭā recalls the lost garden and nest of stanza 1, marking separation from home and freedom.
The present perfect ho gayā hai indicates a completed change whose painful result continues into the present.
The repeated object marker ko keeps the two nouns reversible, so eater and eaten exchange places grammatically and emotionally.
blocks.role: This couplet opens the final stanza: after losing the garden, heart and grief now consume each other.

ur: گانا اسے سمجھ کر خوش ہوں نہ سُننے والے
دُکھّے ہوئے دلوں کی فریاد یہ صدا ہے
roman: gānā use samajh kar ḳhush hūñ na sunne vāle
dukhe hue diloñ kī fariyād ye sadā hai
poetic: Listeners, do not be glad, taking it for a song—
This voice is the lament of wounded hearts.
notes: The couplet sets gānā (song) against fariyād (lament) and sadā (voice/cry), correcting a mishearing: the bird's sound is pain, not entertainment.
Addressing sunne vāle (listeners) directly shifts the poem from private memory to public warning.
Dukhe hue diloñ (wounded hearts) broadens the speaker's individual grief into a collective cry of all suffering hearts.
In Iqbal's allegorical register, the caged bird's cry can be the voice of a colonized or spiritually captive people.
blocks.role: Turns personal lament into universal cry; warns listeners not to aestheticize suffering, preparing the final appeal to the captor.

ur: آزاد مجھ کو کر دے، او قید کرنے والے!
مَیں بے زباں ہوں قیدی، تو چھوڑ کر دُعا لے
roman: āzād mujh ko kar de o qaid karne vāle
maiñ be zabāñ hūñ qaidī tū chhoṛ kar duʿā le

phrases.gloss: set free — compound verb āzād karnā in the imperative

poetic: Set me free, O you who keep me confined!
I am a mute prisoner — release me, and earn my prayer.
notes: The compound verb āzād kar de means "set free"; the object mujh ko is inserted between its parts, as is normal in Urdu compound verbs.
Qaid karne vāle literally means "one who does imprisonment" — the captor or jailer; allegorically this may be God, fate, or the colonizer.
Be zabāñ literally means "without tongue" — the bird cannot plead its case; it also evokes the silencing of the colonized or the soul in bondage.
Duʿā le turns the plea into a moral transaction: by releasing the captive, the captor earns a prayer or blessing from him.
The intimate tū addresses the captor both boldly and intimately, as one might address God or a powerful adversary.
blocks.role: Final direct appeal to the captor: the mute prisoner asks for freedom, offering its prayer as the captor's reward.

context_notes.text: be zabāñ literally means 'without a tongue'; it is the common Urdu expression for mute or voiceless.
duʿā means a prayer or blessing; receiving someone's duʿā is considered a spiritual reward.
